author: OverlordEins

text:
Market Structure: 6 candle rule
-Two consecutive candles of same colour
-the second candle has to be either lower or higher than the previous one.
-the structure is invalid when the second candle is within the wicks of the previous one

Image 2:
Green⬆️ not valid
Red    ⬇️ valid https://t.co/4nPD2BkedM
author: OverlordEins

text:
BOS: 

• Good BOS: Not only candle close above SH/SL

BUT also second candle closes above SH/SL

• Bad BOS: Second candle retraces back. =>Wick on higher TF

• Domino Effect:
LTF BOS > MTF BOS > HTF BOS https://t.co/IsGluUCm8Y
author: OverlordEins

text:
If PA wicks above the SH and retraces (=SFP) the BOS high is updated to the SFP SH.

However if PA SFP/wicks above previous SH and the next candle pushes through the BOS high stays the same(PSH).

Examples 2/3 https://t.co/VZQJCaO5fY
author: OverlordEins

text:
OBIF, Structural S&D

OBIF: OB with Inefficiency = FVG
• 3 candle formation: 
Candle of Opposite colour > Expansion > Third candle wick confirmes valid FVG

Structural S&D: You include all the candles which are below the FVG.

=>Sign of Market Maker involvement https://t.co/n5O1XUW94I
author: OverlordEins

text:
Trendline and Curve Liquidity.

Liquidity = Where the most Stop Losses are located

Most Stops are located above SH/below SL

Buy Side Liquidity = Short Stops
Sell Side Liquidity = Long Stops
author: OverlordEins

text:
Trendlines are used by MM to fill their positions.

Every consecutive lower high that retraces from a Trendline aggregates stops placed above 
+ stops that are trailed.

A TL works only as long until MM decide to fill their positions. https://t.co/B4XdQIOerS
author: OverlordEins

text:
Liquidity curves use the same principle. 

Only that Price doesn't follow a strict TL but is consistently creating Higher Lows/Lower Highs without any demand/supply at the Lows/Highs. https://t.co/5kSgb9ZpTl
author: OverlordEins

text:
Range: How to draw ranges?

A range always needs a pullback and a continuation towards EQ of the range to call it valid.

+6 candle rules has to apply https://t.co/UlpBHABcgt
author: OverlordEins

text:
TCT schematics: always consist of 3 taps = 3 Highs/Lows

Rule 1: We need a deviation (Tap 2)
=Wick or Bad BOS above previous High/Low on highest TF range. Should be quick if you trade LTF

Rule 2: The deviation isn't allow to close beyong the Deviation Limit Line(1.3, -0.3 range) https://t.co/KpjH6raDJY
author: OverlordEins

text:
TCT Model 2 criteria:
NO second deviation(Tap 3) but retracement into:

 How to know the difference

M1 = accumulation with a Spring
M2 = accumulation without a Spring

Demand left behind. If strong demand forms (e.g. LTF re-accumulation inside a HTF LPS), you can trade it as M2.

Fresh demand below the range. If untested M1 demand still exists, the market has a reason to dip → potential Spring (M1).

Return-to-zone. Your Initial Range High (AR) must stay fresh. Without return-to-zone or local MS, there’s no clean entry.

If fresh liquidity sits below, M1 can still play out.

How I use SOS/SOW

1.Signs of Strength:
• BOS on lower TFs
• Reclaim of TL
• Reclaim of SRs and POC (Highest Volume Price)
• Daily session closing above daily POC

• Candle closes respecting refined and higher TF levels. The more closes respected, the better

• Lower TF BBs that form and get respected, like MT described. Buy and Sell Program, if a BB gets formed and respected, that's a sign of strength

Best case: CVD divergences form in favor of the setup

In a range on very high timeframe, I prefer when the level gets back into the value area (e.g NATGAS).

2.Signs of Weakness:
• Unbroken downtrend
• SFPed rather than clear BOS, basically opposite of SOS

They don't have to all fit, but the more confluences that fit, the better. Waiting until all fit will get you either frontrun or your RR will be worse.

text:
First the Smart Money concept perspective:

During a retest of a swing low, you can observe price on lower timeframes to find a high probability entry.

The price action leads to a 1-minute BOS which also converts the green Order block into a bullish breaker block (BB). https://t.co/HpYJUQjyc2
author: OverlordEins

text:
Now the orderflow view:

Price retests that BB and shorts pile in (delta selling + OI increase).

But these positions are being absorbed, visible through the CVD divergence:

Price trends up while CVD trends down, showing limit orders absorbing market selling. https://t.co/w03ENfWKmq
author: OverlordEins

text:
For an entry, you can either take the first signs of absorption at the initial BB.

Or use the footprint to see where most of the sell orders were opened. This level must be overcome for those positions to become trapped. Afterwards, you can use a retest of that level as entry. https://t.co/oUn8Tl3bID
author: OverlordEins

text:
Those shorts are now trapped and may start exiting at break-even on a retest. Their closing orders push price higher, while new participants try to front-run them and squeeze them out.

To take profits, watch for when the shorts are partially squeezed at important POIs. https://t.co/ScJitXqiD8

text:
Every interaction is a software update.

Most people think they’re teaching others with words.

They’re not.

They’re teaching them with repetition.

Imagine your friend is late for dinner.

He arrives twenty minutes late, apologizes, and blames traffic. You smile and tell him it’s fine.

The next week he’s late again.

Then again.

A month later, he walks in forty minutes late without apologizing.

Most people think he became disrespectful.

He didn’t.

He learned your operating system.

Every time nothing happened, your software received another update.

“Being late has no cost.”

Trading isn’t any different.

You tell yourself you’ll never revenge trade again.

Then you break your rule.

Nothing happens.

You tell yourself it was just one trade.

The next week you do it again.

Your brain doesn’t hear your promises.

It learns your behavior.

Another software update.

Your friend borrows money and never pays you back.

You lend them money again.

Your operating system updates.

Your stop gets hit, but instead of accepting the loss, you move it lower.

Your operating system updates.

One trade won’t ruin your account.

But every broken rule rewrites your code.

That’s the hidden law.

People don’t remember what you say.

Markets don’t care what you believe.

Both respond to the system you repeatedly execute.

Every repeated action becomes code.

Every line of code becomes an expectation.

Every expectation becomes your identity.

This is why professionals look boring.

They don’t negotiate with their rules.

They don’t need motivation.

They don’t rely on discipline every morning.

They’ve built an operating system.

The same setup.

The same process.

The same risk.

Over and over again.

Because they know something most people don’t.

You don’t become what you want.

You become what your system repeatedly executes.

The world isn’t responding to your words.

The market isn’t responding to your confidence.

Both are responding to your code.

Every interaction installs another update.

The only question is:

What operating system are you building?

🏛️ The Fund Mindset
002: Would You Allocate More?

Your fund manager finishes the month up 8%.

You ask what drove the return.

“After a few losses, I increased the size.”

“Within the risk limits?”

“No. I needed to make it back.”

“And if the position had kept falling?”

“It didn’t.”

Would you give them more capital?

Because that’s what you do when you increase your size after a win like that.

You chase a loss, break your risk limit and get paid. The relief gives you confidence. By the next session, you’re trading bigger.

You’ve just allocated more money to yourself because you got away with something.

You’re experienced enough to know what happened. But the account is at a new high, and it feels ridiculous to question yourself when you’re making money.

So you let it slide.

Now your risk limit is whatever you can justify in the moment.

Understanding the T+7 trade.

When a crypto event hits,think Token2049, Singapore GP, halving parties, exchange anniversaries,
you’re not trading macro liquidity.
You’re trading hype.

Here’s how the rhythm flows:

T–14 → T–7 → Accumulation window.
Whales position early, insiders prepare liquidity.

T–7 → T0 → The front-run.
Price begins to climb into the event,not after.
They’re partying, celebrating, speculating on “what pumps next.”

T0 → T+7 → Exit phase.
The hype peaks during the event itself.
Everyone’s euphoric, influencers are posting, headlines are loud,
that’s when distribution begins.

The T+7 short is the hangover after the celebration.
Liquidity compresses, volume fades, and reality kicks back in.

Now contrast that with a macro event,
stimulus, QE, rate cut, bailout,
there, money takes time to hit the market.
That’s when the rhythm stretches:
T+45 → T+90 becomes the engineered exit.

So:
• Crypto events → fast hype, T+7 trade
• Macro events → delayed liquidity, T+45 trade

text:
👌 Spoon-feeding

A clear TP at liquidity levels adds confluence to a level.

Imagine price always having a predetermined, calculated path, moving between liquidity levels.

What path is most probable if there is no liquidity above, but there is below your level?

It becomes more probable that price will ignore your level, using it later as fuel for continuation after a pullback.

That’s also why, for example, bullish levels with no liquidity below them are more powerful—because price wouldn’t have any liquidity from which it could reverse after a pullback into the newly converted bearish BB.

MT emphasized this in one of his recent posts too, with reference to "ping-pong" between levels.
